title: Data manipulation
Data manipulation
text:
Packages
The tidyverse is a set of packages that share one style. Install it once, load it in every file:

install.packages("tidyverse")   # once, in the console
library(tidyverse)              # at the top of every document


Tidy data:

each row is an observation;
each column is a variable;
each cell is a single value.

text:
Summaries by group
In session 1 we computed a mean for each group, one group at a time. group_by() and summarise() do all groups at once:

penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n         = n(),
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_mass   = sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Data manipulation
text:
Describing a numeric variable: centre








Summary
What it says
R




mean
the average: the sum divided by \(n\)
mean(x)


median
the middle value: half below, half above
median(x)


percentile
the 25th percentile has 25% of the values below it
quantile(x, 0.25)




The median is the 50th percentile. The 25th and 75th are the quartiles.
Missing values? Add na.rm = TRUE, as before.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Describing a numeric variable: spread








Summary
What it says
R




range
from the smallest to the largest value
min(x), max(x)


middle half
from the 25th to the 75th percentile
quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75))


variance
the average squared distance from the mean
var(x)


standard deviation
the square root of the variance, in the units of the data
sd(x)



The more the values differ from each other, the larger all four.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Seeing them

Body mass is right-skewed: a tail of heavy penguins pulls the mean above the median.

text:
Summaries by group, all together

penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean   = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    p25    = quantile(body_mass, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    p75    = quantile(body_mass, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    min    = min(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    max    = max(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd     = sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  <fct>     <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <int> <int> <dbl>

2 Chinstrap 3733.   3700 3488.  3950  2700  4800  384.
3 Gentoo    5076.   5000 4700   5500  3950  6300  504.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Work inside an R Project
Before reading any data, organise your work in an RStudio Project: a folder that contains your scripts and your data.

File > New Project... in RStudio creates the project folder.
Move your data files inside that folder, for example in data/.


The here package builds file paths from the project folder: no C:/Users/... paths, no setwd(). The same code runs on any computer.

library(here)
here("data", "questionnaire.xlsx")   # <project>/data/questionnaire.xlsx

title: Data manipulation
text:
Reading Excel files: read_xlsx()
Excel files (.xls, .xlsx) need the readxl package:

library(readxl)
answers <- read_xlsx(here("data", "questionnaire.xlsx"))


An Excel file can contain several sheets. Pick one with the sheet argument:

answers <- read_xlsx(here("data", "questionnaire.xlsx"), sheet = "day_1")

For .csv files: read_csv(), from the tidyverse.

title: Data manipulation
text:
Save your results
Use here() to write files into your project too. Take a result like:

my_res <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_bill = mean(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE))
my_res

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   mean_bill
  <fct>         <dbl>
1 Adelie         38.8
2 Chinstrap      48.8
3 Gentoo         47.5

title: Data manipulation
text:
Save to a file
As an R file, to use again in R:

write_rds(my_res, here("my_results.rds"))   # save
my_res <- read_rds(here("my_results.rds"))  # load next time

As an Excel file:

library(writexl)
write_xlsx(my_res, here("my_results.xlsx"))

title: Data manipulation
text:
Inconsistent column names
Real files rarely have tidy names: spaces, random capitals, dots…

raw <- data.frame(`Participant ID` = c("P01", "P02"),
                  `Age (years)` = c(23, 31),
                  `Reaction.Time` = c(512, 430),
                  check.names = FALSE)  # keep the messy names
raw

  Participant ID Age (years) Reaction.Time
1            P01          23           512
2            P02          31           430



clean_names() from the janitor package makes them all lower case, with _ between words:

library(janitor)
clean_names(raw)

  participant_id age_years reaction_time
1            P01        23           512
2            P02        31           430

title: Data manipulation
text:
Missing values
Missing entries are stored as NA:

my_df

  id    group sleep_hours mood
1  1  control         7.0    6
2  2 exercise         6.5   NA
3  3  control          NA    7
4  4 exercise         8.0    8
5  5  control         5.5    4



Find them with is.na():

is.na(my_df$sleep_hours)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE


Any operation involving NA returns NA: pass na.rm = TRUE to summaries such as mean().

title: Data manipulation
text:
Joining data frames

left_join(): all rows from x
right_join(): all rows from y
full_join(): all rows from both x and y
inner_join(): only rows with a match in both
semi_join(): rows from x with a match in y, keeping only x’s columns
anti_join(): rows from x with no match in y

Animations on the next slides: tidyexplain, by Garrick Aden-Buie.

title: Introduction
section: From a sample to general conclusions
text:
From a sample to general conclusions
We observe a tiny portion of the world, e.g. a few subjects, sessions, trials.
We want conclusions that hold in general.

Statistics quantifies how much we can generalise despite

measurement noise (instruments, questionnaires);
variability between and within subjects;
factors we did not measure.

title: Introduction
text:
Aims
Study of populations

100 subjects scanned once: population across individuals.
1 subject scanned daily for a year: population across time.


Study of variation

Variability between subjects, across time, across space.



Data reduction

From millions of numbers per subject to summaries (means, components, features).

Fisher (1925), Statistical Methods for Research Workers, ch. 1

title: Introduction
text:
Pay attention!
Classical tools (t-test, ANOVA, regression) assume independent observations.

Neuroscience data often are not:

10 trials from one subject are more similar than 10 trials from 10 subjects;
the same questionnaire filled in 6 times by one participant gives correlated scores.



Ignoring this leads to overconfidence (underestimation of uncertainty)
A standard tool to deal with correlated responses is mixed models, but we will not cover them in this course.

title: Introduction
text:
The reproducibility crisis

Reproducibility: same data and same analysis give the same results.
Replication: new data on the same question give consistent results.



Nature survey of 1,576 researchers: more than 70% had tried and failed to replicate another scientist’s experiments, more than half their own (Baker, 2016).
70 teams analysed the same brain-imaging data to test the same 9 hypotheses. No two teams used the same workflow, and their results varied considerably (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020).

title: Introduction
text:
Why studies fail to replicate
Common threats: low statistical power, trying analyses until something is significant (p-hacking), hypotheses made up after seeing the results, unpublished null results, no shared data or code (Munafò et al., 2017).

title: Introduction
text:

State the hypothesis before looking at the data.
Share raw data and code. Every number in the paper generated automatically.
Write reports where text, code and results live together.



This is why we analyse data with code.
